claim: On PaLM 2 with 692 binary forecasting questions, none of the structured strategies (Breakdown, Base Rates, Both Sides, Crowd, News API) beat the plain prompt on unweighted Brier; test Brier: Basic 0.1062, Base Rates 0.1233, Breakdown 0.1815.
quote: none of the more complex forecasting strategies outperform the most basic baseline
title: Can Language Models Use Forecasting Strategies?
transfer: Gate any forecasting procedure: do not force base-rate or decomposition steps by default; compare against a plain answer at equal tokens before enabling.

claim: The plain prompt's edge in that study is partly a label artifact: about 63% of questions resolved No and the plain prompt gave lower probabilities. On a Weighted Brier that scores Yes and No resolutions separately, the human baseline beat all LLM methods.
quote: the human baseline outperforms all LLM methods
title: Can Language Models Use Forecasting Strategies?
transfer: Always score calibration on a class-balanced metric as well as plain Brier, or the step that merely shifts the base rate will look good or bad by accident.

claim: In the Halawi system on 914 test questions, the full pipeline scored Brier 0.179 vs crowd 0.149 and best zero-shot or scratchpad baseline 0.208-0.209. Removing fine-tuning gave 0.186; removing fine-tuning and retrieval gave 0.206. The reasoning prompt (which mentions base rates) was never ablated alone, and the paper calls its gain minor.
quote: our system's Brier score (.179) significantly outperforms the best baseline model (.208 with GPT-4-1106-Preview)
title: Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models
venue: arXiv:2402.18563 (preprint; NeurIPS 2024 per my memory, not verified)
transfer: Retrieval gave the big gain (0.206 to 0.186); prompt structure gave little. Spend extra calls on getting facts, not on reasoning templates.

claim: Gap 1 status: the two direct tests found no isolated benefit of base-rate or decomposition prompting for LLMs. Pratt found it worse than plain; Halawi never isolated it. No equal-compute test showing a gain was found.
authors: Pratt et al. 2024; Halawi et al. 2024
title: see d-01 and d-03
transfer: Treat reference-class and decomposition as optional steps behind a gate, not as defaults.

claim: CHECK: Is it supported that reference class / decomposition prompting helps LLM forecasting? Verdict: not supported by the evidence found. Pratt 2024 (PaLM 2) shows it hurts or ties; Halawi 2024 did not isolate it. The web search budget ran out, so later work (2025) was not searched and may differ.
transfer: none

claim: Semantic entropy (Farquhar 2024, Nature 630:625-630) averaged AUROC 0.790 over 30 task-model combinations vs naive entropy 0.691, P(True) 0.698, embedding regression 0.687, on LLaMA, Falcon, Mistral 7B to 70B. Its AUROC is a lower bound because it counts all errors, not only confabulations.
title: Detecting hallucinations in large language models using semantic entropy
n: 30 task-model combinations; biography test 21 people, 150 claims
transfer: For short-answer sub-questions, sample k answers, cluster by meaning, and use cluster entropy as an escalate-or-doubt signal. Costs k extra calls.

claim: Semantic entropy only targets confabulation from missing knowledge. It does not catch confident errors from training-data misconceptions, reward-driven deception or systematic reasoning failures. Its evaluation used GPT-4 as grader and withheld context, and covered open-weight models, not Claude.
title: Detecting hallucinations in large language models using semantic entropy
transfer: Do not read low entropy as 'correct'. It is a weak-knowledge detector only. Same-model samples that agree can still share a wrong belief.

claim: Semantic entropy needs about 5 to 10 times more compute from extra samples; Semantic Entropy Probes approximate it from one generation's hidden states. Probes need hidden states, so not available to an API-only agent.
authors: Kossen, Han, Razzak, Schut, Malik, Gal
title: Semantic Entropy Probes: Robust and Cheap Hallucination Detection in LLMs
transfer: With an API model, the sampling form is the only option; budget 5 to 10 calls per checked claim.

claim: CHECK: Farquhar 2024 is a real peer-reviewed Nature paper, so the earlier citation is confirmed. It is a single group's result by the same lab as Kuhn 2023 and Kossen 2024, so it is not an independent replication. No independent replication on Claude-class models was found (search budget ran out).
transfer: none

claim: Reasoning models were better calibrated than non-reasoning counterparts in 33 of 36 settings, on both factual sets (TriviaQA, NonambigQA) and reasoning sets (SuperGPQA, MMLU-Pro, math and non-math), 1,000 examples each. Models tested were open-weight pairs (for example GLM, EXAONE, R1-Distill), not Claude.
authors: Yoon, Kim, Yang, Kim, Kim, Kim, Choi, Kim, Seo
title: Reasoning Models Better Express Their Confidence
transfer: none

claim: In the Yoon slow-thinking ablation on R1-Distill-Qwen-32B, removing non-linear reasoning (exploring alternatives, backtracking) hurt calibration most: TriviaQA ECE 0.042 to 0.161; no CoT gave 0.150. Removing epistemic markers raised ECE but raised AUROC.
quote: Non-linear Reasoning has the greatest impact on calibration
title: Reasoning Models Better Express Their Confidence
transfer: Before stating confidence, require the agent to try an alternative answer and say what would make it wrong. Supports a doubt step for confidence reports, not for the answer itself.

claim: Mei 2025 tested Claude 3.7 Sonnet, DeepSeek R1, Gemini 2.0 Flash Thinking and o3-mini on ARC-Challenge, GPQA, MMLU subsets, StrategyQA and SimpleQA (mostly factual or knowledge). Reasoning depth raised calibration error where accuracy did not rise (SimpleQA) and raised confidence on questions always answered wrongly. On GPQA, deeper reasoning helped when accuracy rose.
quote: deeper reasoning makes reasoning models more confident in their incorrect responses
authors: Mei, Zhang, Yin, Lidard, Shorinwa, Majumdar
title: Reasoning about Uncertainty: Do Reasoning Models Know When They Don't Know?
n: 4 models, 5 benchmarks; depth tested on 2 models
transfer: Do not trust longer thinking to improve confidence. Where accuracy does not move with depth, extra reasoning inflates certainty. Add outside checks, not more of the same reasoning.

claim: Among the four models in Mei 2025, Claude 3.7 Sonnet was the best calibrated and its calibration error rose only about 2 points from low to high reasoning (o3-mini about 7). Asking Claude to reflect on its own uncertainty made it worse, especially on StrategyQA and SimpleQA.
quote: Claude is the most calibrated model by a significant margin
title: Reasoning about Uncertainty: Do Reasoning Models Know When They Don't Know?
transfer: For a Claude agent, use the raw verbalised confidence from a direct elicitation and do not add a 'reflect on your uncertainty' pass without a measured gain.

claim: CHECK: Do Yoon and Mei conflict? Verdict: mostly no. They ask different questions. Yoon compares reasoning vs non-reasoning model pairs; Mei varies depth within reasoning models and tests introspection. Both include factual QA, so a factual vs math split does not explain it. Mei's extra overconfidence is tied to cases where accuracy stays flat. Both are preprints and neither is a Claude-4-class test. Claude 3.7 was the best calibrated in Mei.
transfer: none

claim: Across 350+ LLMs on two leaderboards and a resume task, errors are substantially correlated: when two models both err they give the same wrong answer about 60% of the time on one dataset. Correlation rises with shared architecture or provider, and larger more accurate models are more correlated.
title: Correlated Errors in Large Language Models
transfer: Treat agreement among samples as weak evidence, especially from one model. Extremizing an aggregate of one-model samples is not justified. This is cross-model data; within-model correlation is likely higher.

claim: A crowd of 12 LLMs was not statistically different from 925 humans on 31 binary questions, with a strong yes-bias. Showing GPT-4 and Claude 2 the human median improved accuracy 17% to 28%, but averaging human and machine forecasts was better.
quote: the LLM crowd outperforms a simple no-information benchmark and is not statistically different from the human crowd
title: Wisdom of the Silicon Crowd: LLM Ensemble Prediction Capabilities Rival Human Crowd Accuracy
transfer: Ensembling across different models gave the crowd effect. Diversity came from different models, not different samples of one. If only one model is available, vary the retrieved facts and framing, and test it.

claim: CHECK: Does a confidence signal survive when all voters are one model? Verdict: no direct measurement found. Indirect: Kim 2025 shows high cross-model correlation, and Schoenegger's crowd effect came from 12 different models. Pratt 2024 'Crowd' persona averaging on one model (PaLM 2) did not beat the plain prompt (test Brier 0.1611 vs 0.1062). Gap 2 stays open.
transfer: none

claim: A TACL survey of abstention in LLMs organises methods by query, model and human values and lists open directions, including whether abstention can be a general skill and tuning it per context. It is a survey, not a test of a confidence-based router on open-ended agent tasks.
authors: Wen, Yao, Feng, Xu, Tsvetkov, Howe, Wang
title: Know Your Limits: A Survey of Abstention in Large Language Models
transfer: Escalation rules are an open area. Build one as a measured step: escalate when sampled answers split into several meaning clusters, and test the rule on our own tasks.

claim: CHECK: Is there evidence on confidence routing for open-ended tasks? Verdict: not found. Only a survey was opened (abstract level). Gap 4 stays open; the search budget ran out before more could be sought.
transfer: none

claim: CHECK: Mellers 2014 training effect size and the 2019 Journal of Politics teams study could not be verified. The SAGE page returned HTTP 403 and web search was unavailable. No new number is added; the earlier snippet-level status stays, and the 'Journal of Politics 2019' citation from the earlier brief remains unconfirmed and should not be cited.
transfer: none

claim: CHECK: Is the Brier gain from retrieval larger than from prompt structure in LLM forecasting? Verdict: supported by one preprint. In Halawi 2024, removing retrieval moved Brier from 0.186 to 0.206 (back to baseline), while the reasoning prompt gave a minor gain. Single source.
title: Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models
transfer: none
